decks.domain: Emergency situations: collision avoidance, ABS, skids, drop-offs, vehicle malfunctions, breakdowns and emergency contact records

cards.front: What responsibility does every driver have toward collisions?
cards.back: Every driver has the responsibility to do everything possible to prevent collisions.

cards.front: Why does being prepared for emergencies matter?
cards.back: Most drivers will face an emergency sooner or later, and being prepared may let you prevent a serious outcome.

cards.front: What are the three options for avoiding a collision?
cards.back: You have three options for avoiding a collision or reducing its impact: braking, steering or accelerating.

cards.front: What is most drivers' first instinct when a collision threatens?
cards.back: For most drivers the first instinct when a collision threatens is to stop the vehicle.

cards.front: What does an anti-lock braking system let you do?
cards.back: Most new vehicles have an anti-lock braking system, or ABS, which lets you stop without skidding while keeping steering control, so read your owner's manual on how to use it.

cards.front: How should you press the brake in a vehicle with ABS?
cards.back: With ABS, press the brake pedal as hard as you can and hold constant pressure, and do not pump the brakes, because pumping deactivates ABS.

cards.front: How does correct ABS braking differ from pumping the brakes?
cards.back: ABS braking means firm, constant pressure on the pedal, the opposite of pumping, which would switch ABS off.

cards.front: What should you expect to feel or hear when ABS is working?
cards.back: ABS works only while you keep pressure on the pedal, and a vibrating pedal or a clicking sound during ABS braking is normal.

cards.front: Can you steer while ABS is active?
cards.back: You can still steer your vehicle while ABS is active.

cards.front: How should you brake in a vehicle without ABS?
cards.back: If your vehicle has no ABS, follow your owner's manual for the right braking procedure.

cards.front: What is swerving, and when can it help?
cards.back: Quickly steering around a problem, sometimes called swerving, may let you avoid a collision.

cards.front: How do you swerve correctly?
cards.back: To swerve, hold the steering wheel firmly with both hands and steer the way you want to go while trying to avoid other traffic.

cards.front: What do you do once you are past the problem in a swerve?
cards.back: Once past the problem, steer the opposite way to straighten the vehicle, regain control and settle at a suitable speed.

cards.front: What two steering moves make up a swerve?
cards.back: A swerve has two steering moves: first toward where you want to go, then back the opposite way to straighten out once the problem is cleared.

cards.front: When might accelerating help you avoid a collision?
cards.back: Accelerating may be the way to avoid a collision, for example when another vehicle is about to hit you from behind or from the side.

cards.front: Besides braking and swerving, what else can avoid a collision?
cards.back: Braking and swerving are not the only escapes, because speeding up may be what avoids a vehicle about to strike you from behind or the side.

cards.front: What causes a skid?
cards.back: Skids happen when you drive too fast for road conditions, stop suddenly or the tires can no longer grip the road, and once skidding you have little control.
cards.memory_hook: Too fast, sudden stop, no grip

cards.front: What should you do if your vehicle starts to skid?
cards.back: If your vehicle starts to skid, ease off the brake or accelerator, look where you want to go and steer in that direction.

cards.front: What is panic steering at a drop-off?
cards.back: Avoid panic steering, which is trying to get back onto the pavement the instant the wheels leave it at an uneven drop-off.

cards.front: How do you recover if a drop-off takes you off the pavement?
cards.back: If an uneven drop-off takes your vehicle off the paved surface, slow down gradually when it is safe and steer gently back onto the pavement.

cards.front: Why should you leave and return to the road gradually?
cards.back: Going off and coming back onto the road gradually, with only slight steering, reduces the chance of erratic vehicle behavior on an uneven or unpaved shoulder.

cards.front: Why are uneven surface drop-offs dangerous?
cards.back: Uneven surface drop-offs can cause serious collisions when a driver reacts the wrong way.

cards.front: What is the safe response at a drop-off, and what is the dangerous one?
cards.back: At a drop-off the safe response is a gradual slowdown and gentle steering back on, while the dangerous one is an immediate jerk back onto the pavement.

cards.front: What greatly reduces the chance of a vehicle problem?
cards.back: Following the maintenance schedule in your owner's manual greatly cuts the chance of a vehicle problem while driving.

cards.front: What does a brake warning light mean?
cards.back: Check all warning lights, including the brake light, because a brake warning light means the brakes are not working properly and you should not drive.
cards.memory_hook: Brake light on, do not drive

cards.front: What should you do first if your brakes fail while driving?
cards.back: If the brakes fail while you drive, use the parking brake, pulling its handle or pushing its pedal slowly so the rear wheels do not lock, and be ready to release it if a skid starts.

cards.front: What if the parking brake also fails?
cards.back: If the parking brake does not work either, turn off the engine, find a safe place to slow to a stop off the roadway, and do not keep driving without working brakes.
cards.memory_hook: Engine off, find a safe stop

cards.front: In what order do you respond to brake failure?
cards.back: For brake failure the parking brake comes first, and turning off the engine is the fallback only if the parking brake also fails.

cards.front: What is a tire blowout, and what does a front blowout do?
cards.back: A tire blowout is a rapid loss of air from a tire, and if a front tire blows out the vehicle pulls sharply toward the side of the blowout.

cards.front: How does a rear tire blowout feel?
cards.back: If a rear tire blows out, the vehicle wobbles, shakes and pulls somewhat toward the side of the blowout.

cards.front: How do front and rear blowouts differ?
cards.back: A front tire blowout pulls the vehicle sharply toward the blown side, while a rear blowout makes it wobble and shake and pull only somewhat.

cards.front: What should you do as soon as a tire blows out?
cards.back: In a blowout or sudden flat, grip the wheel firmly, keep the vehicle going straight and slow down gradually by taking your foot off the accelerator.

cards.front: Should you brake after a blowout?
cards.back: Do not brake after a blowout; let the vehicle slow on its own, or brake gently if you must.

cards.front: Where should you stop after a blowout?
cards.back: Avoid stopping on the road after a blowout if at all possible; pull off in a safe place, turn on the emergency flashers and have the tire changed and replaced.

cards.front: How does braking after a blowout differ from braking after an engine failure?
cards.back: After a blowout you avoid braking and let the vehicle coast down, while after an engine failure you brake with steady pressure rather than hard.

cards.front: What should you know about steering when the engine shuts off?
cards.back: If the engine shuts off while driving, keep a strong grip, knowing the steering wheel may be hard to turn but can still be turned.

cards.front: How should you slow down after an engine failure?
cards.back: After an engine failure, look for an escape path and, instead of braking hard, use steady brake pressure to slow down and pull off the roadway.

cards.front: What should you do once stopped after an engine failure?
cards.back: Once stopped after an engine failure, try to restart it, and if that fails, raise the hood, turn on the emergency flashers and call for help.

cards.front: What should you do first if your vehicle accelerates out of control?
cards.back: If your vehicle is accelerating out of control, the manual says to turn off the engine, shift to neutral and search for an escape path.

cards.front: How does the stuck accelerator response differ from engine failure?
cards.back: For a stuck accelerator the printed order is engine off, then neutral, then an escape path, which differs from the restart attempt used after an engine failure.

cards.front: How do you finish handling a stuck accelerator?
cards.back: With a stuck accelerator, steer smoothly, brake gently, pull off the roadway and have the pedal repaired at a service center before driving again.

cards.front: Why must a broken-down vehicle be visible?
cards.back: If your vehicle breaks down on the highway, make sure others can see it, since collisions often happen when a driver notices a disabled vehicle too late to stop.
cards.memory_hook: Be seen before it is late

cards.front: How can you report a breakdown?
cards.back: If you have a cell phone or other device, use it to tell authorities that your vehicle, or another one, has broken down.

cards.front: What should you do if you must stop with vehicle trouble?
cards.back: If you must stop with vehicle trouble, get off the road and away from traffic if possible and turn on your emergency flashers.

cards.front: Where should emergency flares be placed?
cards.back: If you carry emergency flares, set them about two hundred to three hundred feet behind the vehicle so other drivers have time to change lanes.

cards.front: How do flashers and flares differ in purpose?
cards.back: Flashers show your vehicle is disabled, while flares placed well behind it give approaching drivers time to change lanes.

cards.front: Who can enter emergency contact information on their SCDMV record?
cards.back: Holders of a beginner's permit, driver's license or identification card can enter emergency contact information on their SCDMV record through the dmv.sc.gov website.

cards.front: Who can see your emergency contact information after a collision?
cards.back: After a collision or medical emergency, South Carolina law enforcement officers can then see that emergency contact information and may share it with medical personnel.

recap_hooks.text: You can brake, steer or accelerate to avoid a collision, and with ABS you press hard and hold steady without pumping.
In a skid, ease off the pedals, look where you want to go and steer that way.
At a drop-off, slow gradually and ease back on, and if the brakes fail, use the parking brake first.
After a blowout, grip firmly, go straight and let the vehicle slow without braking.
With a stuck accelerator, turn off the engine and shift to neutral, and when broken down, use flashers and flares to be seen.
